h1: Beer menu engineering so the best margin beers sell more
title: Beer Menu Engineering for Better Margins | Craft Beer School
desc: How to engineer a taproom or brewpub beer menu: margin per pour, the four-box matrix, layout, pour sizes and staff recommendations.
teaser: Your best-selling beer may be your worst earner. Menu engineering shows you which beers pay the rent.
standfirst: A beer menu is a sales tool. Where a beer sits, how it is described and what sizes it comes in all shape what guests order. Menu engineering uses your own sales data to make the most profitable beers easier to choose.
sections:
Menu engineering begins with a number most taprooms do not track: contribution margin per serve. That is the selling price of a pour minus the cost of the beer in it, including excise duty, ingredients, packaging or keg costs and a fair allowance for loss. Work it out in rupees, not percentages. A high-percentage margin on a cheap beer can earn less per glass than a lower percentage on a premium one.

Our guides to cost per litre and beer pricing strategy help with the inputs.

Take three months of POS data. For each beer, plot two things: how many pours it sold and its margin per pour. Split each axis at the average. Every beer falls into one of four boxes:

  • Stars: popular and high margin. Protect them, keep them prominent.
  • Workhorses: popular but low margin. Often your easy-drinking lager. Nudge the price or cost, but do not hide them.
  • Puzzles: high margin but slow selling. These are your opportunity. Better placement, description or staff recommendation can move them.
  • Dogs: slow and low margin. Replace them or rethink the recipe.

Our guide to tap list planning with sales data shows how to pull the numbers.

Guests read menus quickly and choose from what they notice first. Put stars and puzzles where eyes land: the top of the list and the first item in each section. Many taprooms list beers from light to strong, which helps guests navigate. Within that order, you can still give a high-margin beer a box, a bold name or a short line of description.

Keep prices aligned in a neat column without leader dots, which encourage price comparison. Many menus also drop the ₹ sign and trailing zeros so the eye stays on the beer rather than the price.

A beer with a vivid, specific description sells better than a name and an ABV. Write one line that tells a guest what they will taste and when they would want it: "Crisp wheat beer with banana and clove, made for the kebab platter." Avoid jargon guests do not know. Our guide to reading a taproom menu shows what guests are looking for.

Pour size changes margin per rupee. Offer a smaller pour, such as 300 ml, alongside a pint so cautious guests can try a premium beer. A tasting flight of four small glasses introduces puzzles to guests who would never order a full pint of them. Many come back for one. Price flights so they earn a fair margin, not as a giveaway.
Staff are part of the menu

The most powerful menu placement is a server's recommendation. Tell staff which beers you want to move this month and why. Train them to describe those beers well and to offer a small taster. A recommendation from a confident server beats any layout trick.
A worked example of the maths

Take two beers: a house lager and a hazy IPA. The lager has the higher margin as a percentage, because it is cheap to brew. The IPA costs more to make but sells at a higher price, so it can still leave more rupees in the till per pint. Work out both per pour: selling price minus all-in cost, including duty and loss.

Now suppose a menu change moves 20 guests a week from the beer that earns less per pour to the one that earns more. The gain is 20 times the difference per pint, every week, without a single extra guest through the door. Over a year that small nudge often adds up to more than a price rise would. Guests do not feel it. Run the sums with your own costs, duty and prices before you redesign anything.
Review, do not set and forget

Re-run the four boxes every quarter. Ingredient costs, duty and guest tastes change. A puzzle that became a star after a menu change tells you the change worked. A star that slips may be a quality issue. Food matters too: our guide to brewpub food menus and margins covers the kitchen side, which works on the same principles.

The numbers are the easy part. Turning them into a menu, a story and a taproom culture that guests return to is the craft. That is where marketing and community work together.
faqs: Using sales and margin data to decide where beers sit on the menu, how they are described and priced, so the most profitable beers sell more.
Should I calculate margin as a percentage or in rupees?
In rupees per pour. A beer with a high percentage margin but a low price can earn less per glass than a premium beer with a lower percentage.
What should I do with high-margin beers that do not sell?
Give them better placement, a clearer description, smaller pour sizes or a place in a flight. Ask staff to recommend them too.
How often should I review the menu?
Every quarter, using fresh sales data and current costs.
